cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en Rapunzel, first collected and published by the Brothers Grim in 1812. Once upon a time, there lived a man and a woman who had long wished for a child, but never had one. But at last, the woman became pregnant. These people had a little window in the back of their house out of which they could see a fair's garden which was full of flowers and herbs of all sorts. But no one dared to enter the garden. One day the woman stood at this window looking down and saw a lovely bed of Rapunzel. She had such a craving for it and yet she knew she could not have any. She fell into distraction and depression. All of this frightened her husband, who asked his wife the reason she was in such a state. If I can't get any of the Rapunzel from the garden behind our house to eat, surely I will die." The man, who loved his wife very much, thought, "I will get her some, whatever the cost." One evening, he climbed over the high wall and quickly dug up a handful of the Rapunzel, which he took home to his wife. The woman made a salad right away and ate it ravenously. The Rapunzel tasted so good, so good to her that she craved it three times as much. The next day, the man saw that there would be no peace. So he went into the garden again, but he was terribly frightened, for there stood the fairy, who viciously scolded him for daring to enter her garden and steal from it. He begged to be excused as best he could, saying that his wife was pregnant and how it would put her in danger to refuse her request. At last the fairy said, "I will be content. You may take as much Rapunzel as you like, so long as you give me the child your wife now carries." Taken by fear, the man agreed to everything. When the woman went into labor, the fairy appeared instantly, named the little girl Rapunzel, and took her away. This Rapunzel became the most beautiful child under the sun. But when she was 12 years old, the fairy locked her in a high tower that had neither door nor stairs, only a small window at the very top. When the fairy wanted to come in, she stood below and called, "Rapunzel, Rapunzel, let your hair down to me." Rapunzel had magnificent hair as fine as spun gold. When the fairy called out, she would untie it, wrap it around a window hook, and the hair would fall 20 L's down, and the fairy would climb up. One day a young son of a king came through the forest where the tower stood. He saw the beautiful Rapunzel standing at the window and heard her singing with such a sweet voice that he fell completely in love with her. But since there was no door in the tower and no ladder could reach high enough, he fell into despair. Every day he went into the forest and one day he saw the fairy come along and say, "Rapunzel, Rapunzel, let down your hair." Then he saw the ladder that led to the tower. He had memorized the words he had to say, and the next day when it was dark, he went to the tower and called up, "Rapunzel, Rapunzel, let down your hair." Then she let her hair go, and when it was at the bottom, he grabbed hold of it and was pulled up. Rapunzel was frightened at first, but soon she liked the young king so well that she agreed with him that he should come to the tower everyday. So they lived merrily and joyfully for quite some time. The fairy didn't find out what was going on until one day Rapunzel said to her, "Tell me, Madame Goel, my little clothes are getting so tight and won't fit anymore. Oh, you godless child, said the fairy. What do I hear from you? Right away, she saw how she had been deceived and was quite furious. Then she took Rapunzel's beautiful hair, wrapped it around her left hand a couple of times, grabbed a pair of scissors with her right hand, and snip snip, it was cut off. Then she banished Rapunzel to a desert where she fared very poorly. After some time, she bore twins, a boy and a girl. But on the same day she had banished Rapunzel, the fairy fastened her cut hair to the hook. That evening, when the king's son came and said, "Rapunzel, Rapunzel, let down your hair." She did let down the hair, but how astonished the prince was when he found the fairy up there instead of his beloved Rapunzel. You know what? The enraged fairy said. Rapunzel is lost to you forever, you villain. Then the prince became completely desperate, and in an instant he threw himself down from the tower. He escaped with his life, but lost the use of both eyes. He wandered sadly through the forest, eating nothing but grass and roots, and doing nothing but weeping. A few years later, he came to the desert where Rapunzel lived miserably with her children. Her voice seemed so familiar to him, and in the blink of an eye, she knew it was him and threw her arms around his neck. Two of her tears fell into his eyes, and they became clear again, and he could see as before.

A chieftain of the people who make their homes in caves had two wives, and each bore him a daughter. But one wife sickened and died, and the chieftain followed soon after. The stepmother raised both the girls. But while she was loving toward her own daughter Jun Lee, she was cruel to her step-daughter who was called Yashen. She made Yashen do the most difficult and unpleasant of the household chores, and the poor girl had only rags to wear. But even her lowly state could not hide the fact that she was kind, clever, and caring. Yes, Shen made friends with a fish that lived in a pool near her home. It was 10 ft long and had beautiful golden eyes and gleaming golden scales. She did not know it, but the fish was a guardian spirit sent by her mother who still watched over her. Although Yashen never had enough to eat for herself, she always managed to find something to feed her beloved friend. Her visits to the pond were her only source of joy. One day, Juni followed Yashen to the pond and saw her talking to the fish. Angry that her stepsister should have any happiness, Jun Lee told her mother what she saw. The stepmother, also resentful that the girl should have anything pleasant in her life, tricked Yashen into giving her the tattered dress she always wore. By disguising herself in Yashen's clothes, the stepmother was able to approach the fish. She drew out a knife and quickly killed it. The body of the beautiful golden fish was dragged back to the cave where the stepmother and Jun Lee ate it for supper. Yes, Shen was devastated when she saw what had become of her friend. She remained inconsolable until the spirit of an old man appeared before her and told her that she should put the bones of the fish in four pots and hide them under the four corners of her bed. In this way, she could still communicate with her guardian spirit, and the bones would grant her wishes so long as she was wise in making requests. and responsible with what she was given. Later on, the New Year's festival drew near. This was a time when the young people of the village found someone to marry. But the stepmother forbade Yashen from going, fearing that her beautiful, kind, and hardworking stepdaughter might hurt Jun Le's chances of finding a husband. Yes was ordered to clean the cave house while the stepmother and her daughter attended the festival. Yes, heartbroken made a secret wish to the bones. Suddenly, she found herself clothed in a gown of green silk and wrapped in a beautiful cloak made of bright blue kingfisher feathers. On her tiny feet were slippers made of gold. The bones told Yashen to go to the festival and enjoy herself, but to be careful to bring back all of the beautiful clothes she was given to wear. Yes walked to the festival and when she arrived everyone was amazed by her beauty, grace and lovely manners. Many whispered that she must be a princess. Yes had a wonderful time at the festival until she saw the face of her stepsister Jun Lee who was beginning to think there was something familiar about the lovely maiden in the blue cloak of feathers. Yes fled the festival knowing that she must get home before she was discovered. As she ran, one of her lovely golden shoes slipped off her foot and was left behind. When she arrived home, she found that the fishbones were silent. They could not speak to her because not all her clothes were returned, and so their magic was not complete. The golden slipper was found by a peasant who traded it to another man who then presented it to the king of the Tohan Islands. The king was amazed by the craftsmanship and beauty of the slipper. He decided that he must marry the woman who owned the shoe and ordered a search for her. Eventually, the king came to the place where the cave dwellers live, and each young woman was asked to try on the slipper. Yes, Shen's stepmother forced her to stay at home, hidden from the view of the king and his entourage. But of course, the slipper fit none of the other young women, including Jun Lee. Devastated, the king put up a pavilion with the slipper on display in hopes of finding the mysterious maiden. Late at night, desperate to regain her ability to speak to the bones, Yashen crept into the pavilion to retrieve the slipper. But she was discovered by a watchful guard and accused of being a thief. Yes, Shan threw herself down and confessed everything to the king about her miserable childhood, about the beautiful golden fish who was her only friend, about its cruel slaughter, and how its bones granted her wishes. The king saw that she was beautiful, honest, and well-mannered. He believed her and allowed her to depart with the slipper. In the morning, the king came to Yes and saw that everything was as she had said. Yes slippers on and was suddenly clothed again in her beautiful jade green dress with the blue cloak of King Fisher feathers. The stepmother sneered that yes was only a slave and that she had stolen the clothes from Jun Lee, the true owner of the shoes. But the king could see the truth. He told Yashen that he wished to marry her and take her to be the queen of the Tohan Islands. She gave her consent and left with the king to live with him happily ever after. The stepmother and Jun Lee were left behind. The stepmother, having lost her slave, now forced her daughter to do all the household work, treating her just as badly as she had treated Yashen. Jun Lee, having been raised to be as selfish as her mother, rebelled against this. The two women lived in misery until one day when they had a quarrel so violent that they caused their cave to collapse, killing them both. [Music]

description:
This story was made up by my grandfather to entertain my dad when he was a little boy. And when I was a little girl, my dad told it to me. Now I tell it to my kids, and I'm happy to share it with you. I have stretched it out a little bit and added some details, but it's more or less the same story that was made up in the 1950's.

This story may be better for playtime than bedtime if your kids find it exciting.

The grandmother ate the cake and drank the wine that Little Red Riding Hood had brought, and Little Red Riding Hood thought to herself, "I shall never again stray from the path into the woods alone if my mother has forbidden it." But Little Red Riding Hood was clever and went straight on her way. She told her grandmother about a wolf that had wished her good day, but whose eyes had looked very wicked. If I hadn't been on the open road, he would have eaten me up. Come, said the grandmother. Let's lock the door so he can't get in. Soon after, the wolf knocked and called out. Open up, grandmother. It's me, Little Red Riding Hood. I've brought you some baked goods. But they kept quiet and didn't open the door. The evil one circled the house several times and finally jumped onto the roof, meaning to wait until Little Red Riding Hood went home in the evening. Then he would sneak up after her and eat her in the dark. But the grandmother knew what he was planning. She looked to a large stone trough sitting at the hearth. "Tatch the bucket, Little Red Riding Hood. Yesterday I cooked sausages. carry the water they were cooked in to the trough. Little Red Riding Hood moved buckets of water until the large trough was completely full. The smell of sausages went up to the wolf's nose. He sniffed and peered down. At last, he stretched his neck so far that he couldn't hold on any longer. He began to slip and slid off the roof and right into the large trough where he drowned. Little Red Riding Hood, however, went home happily and safely. This fairy tale, apart from our oral tradition, we have found surprisingly nowhere else but in Peralt's Chaperon Rouge, which inspired Teik's adaptation.

description:
This is a fireside reading of the first English translation of Little Red Riding Hood. This work was published in 1729 and translated from Charles Perrault's version of the story, which he published in his Mother Goose Tales.

This early version of the tale does not have a happy ending. Both the grandmother and Little Red Riding Hood are devoured, and there is a lengthy Moral at the end which specifically warns young ladies to be aware of themselves while they walk the streets. Sadly, this message is still relevant as Wolves are still out there.

I have preserved the punctuation and spelling from the original text, so you can observe the archaic spellings and the lack of formal punctuation and capitalization that was common to early modern books. Only one copy of this book is known to still exist, and it is in the Harvard University Library. You can view it online here: https://iiif.lib.harvard.edu/manifests/view/drs:474717094$1i

title: The First Little Red Riding Hood from 1000 Years Ago!
fulltitle: The First Little Red Riding Hood from 1000 Years Ago!
description:
This my own translation of "De puella a lupellis servata," a poem written by the scholar Egbert of Liège 1000 years ago. It tells of a girl given a red tunic by her godfather on her baptismal day, and what happens when some wolves go after her while she is wearing it.

In my translation of this text, I have tried to preserve as much of the literal meaning of the poem as possible while trying to respect its structure of 14 syllables per line. As it did not rhyme in a conventional sense, I chose to include some alliteration to give it a more poetic feel. Here is the original Latin text of the poem:

Quod refero, mecum pagenses dicere norunt,
Et non tam mirum quam ualde est credere uerum:
Quidam suscepit sacro de fonte puellam,
Cui dedit et tunicam rubicundo uellere textam.
Quinquagesima sancta fuit babtismatis huius,
Sole sub exorto quinquennis facta puella;
Progreditur uagabunda sui inmemor atque pericli,
Quam lupus inuadens siluestria lustra petiuit
Et catulis predam tulit atque reliquit edendam.
Qui simul aggressi, cum iam lacerare nequirent,
Ceperunt mulcere caput feritate remota
"Hanc tunicam, mures, nolite," infantula dixit,
"Scindere, quam dedit excipiens de fonte patrinus!"
Mitigat inmites animos deus, auctor eorum.

They were made of a strange but very shining metal and were so delicately worked that it seemed impossible that mortal hands could have formed them. Her father likewise could not gaze enough of them. And as her father spoke very harshly to her and even called her a little storyteller, she began to cry bitterly and said, "Oh, what then shall I say?" At this moment, the door opened. Neither father or mother could remember them. Tell them yourself that my nutcracker is your nephew, young Master Drosser of Nuremberg, and that it was he who gave me the crowns. The counselor's face turned very dark and grave, and he muttered, "Stupid pack. Stupid pack." Upon this, the doctor took little Maria upon his knee and said very seriously, "Listen to me, Maria, once and for all. Drive your foolish dreams and nonsense out of your head. If I ever hear you say again that silly ugly Nutcracker is the nephew of Uncle Drosser, I will throw him out of the window and all the rest of your puppets. Miss Clara not accepted. For you may imagine that things so fine and beautiful as those which she had seen are not easily forgotten. Even Fred turned his back upon his sister whenever she spoke of the wonderful kingdom in which she had been so happy, and it is said that he sometimes would mutter between his teeth, "Silly goose!" Stuck in their kept feathers of goosequill and much finer and taller than those of which they had been deprived and permitted them again to blow the Hassar's grand march. Aha! We know best how it stood with their courage when those hateful balls spotted their red coats. Maria was not allowed then to speak any more of her adventures, but the images of that wonderful fairy kingdom played about her in sweet rustling tones. she could bring them all back again whenever she fixed her thoughts steadfastly upon them. And hence it came that instead of playing as she formally did, she would sit silent and thoughtful, musing within herself, for which reason the rest would often scold her and call her a little dreamer. Sometime after this, it happened that the counselor was busy repairing a clock in Dr. Stalbomb's house. It very soon appeared how polite and well bred the young man was, for he had brought Maria a great many handsome play things, the nicest gingerbread and the same sugar figures which the mouse king had bitten to pieces. Maria raised the youth and said softly, "Dear Master Drossme, you are a kind, good-natured young man, and since you rule in such a charming land among such pretty merry people, I will be your bride." With this, Mariam immediately became Drosselmer's betrothed bride. After a year and a day, he came, as I have heard, and carried her away in a golden chariot drawn by silver horses. title: Old Santeclaus with Much Delight - The FIRST Poem Printed about Santa!
fulltitle: Old Santeclaus with Much Delight - The FIRST Poem Printed about Santa!
description:
This poem was published in 1821 in Volume III of The Children's Friend. This book series was published by William B. Gilley, a printer at No. 92 Broadway in New York. This is the first poem ever printed about the modern-day figure of Santa Claus.

It was published two years before Clement Clark Moore's "A Visit from St. Nicholas," which is much better known, probably because it is more fun. Also, some of the rhymes sound odd today because the modern American accent is very different from that of New York more than 200 years ago! 

This poem is meant to provide moral instruction according to the values of the day. And naughty kids don't get a lump of coal in their stockings -- they get a birch switch!!

Dottie's parents are Dasher and Dancer -- and she can't wait to grow up to be just like them! But even though she is too small to pull Santa's big sleigh, there is still something special she can do to help on Christmas Eve.

This story was made up by T.Q. Townsend for her children in December 2023.

Doie wanted to be just like her mother and father when she grew up. She would dash along in front of her house and then jump dancing in the air, pretending to fly like the big reindeer. It was that a shoemaker had become so poor through no fault of his own, that at last he had nothing left but enough leather for a single pair of shoes. In the morning, after he had said his prayers and was about to sit down to work, he saw the shoes on his table fully finished. He stood in wonderment and didn't know what to say. He liked the shoes so much that he paid more than usual for them. With the money, the shoemaker was able to buy enough leather to make two pairs of shoes. He cut out the pieces in the evening and was very eager to get to work in the morning. But he didn't need to do a thing, for when he got up, the shoes were all done, and there was no shortage of shoppers who left him with enough money to buy leather for four pairs of shoes. Early the next morning, he found the four pairs finished, and so it went. The leather he cut out in the evening was finished by morning. Soon the shoemaker had a good income again, and at last he became a wealthy man.
